power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Objective: To examine whether longitudinal changes in frontoparietal (FP)-subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) joint temporal complexity differ between sgACC hemispheres in patients undergoing accelerated TMS (aTMS) and untreated healthy controls.
Methods: Twenty-four patients with current depressive episodes and fifteen healthy controls underwent 7T resting-state fMRI at baseline and follow-up.
Patients received aTMS localized to the left DLPFC using Beam-F3.
The same bilateral FP time series was paired separately with left and right sgACC time series.
Bivariate multiscale sample entropy (bMSE) across scale factors a1-a10 was summarized by trapezoidal integration as a complexity index (bMSE-CI).
The primary test was the Group × Time × sgACC Hemisphere interaction in a mixed repeatedmeasures ANOVA.
Scale-specific interactions and clinical Spearman correlations were evaluated with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction.
Change scores were follow-up minus baseline.
Results: The bMSE-CI Group × Time × Hemisphere interaction was significant (F(1,37) = 6.043, p = 0.0188, partial η² = 0.140).
Mean left/right bMSE-CI changes were -0.286/+0.124 in patients and +0.323/+0.112 in controls.
Of ten scale-specific three-way interactions, only a2 survived FDR correction (q = 0.0435).
No baseline or change-score bMSE-MADRS association survived the specified FDR corrections.
A random-intercept-only mixed-model sensitivity analysis did not reach statistical significance for the three-way interaction (p = 0.0718).
Conclusion: FP-sgACC joint temporal complexity showed hemisphere-dependent longitudinal differences between patients undergoing aTMS and healthy controls.
These exploratory findings motivate further evaluation of bMSE as a candidate measure of longitudinal neural change in depression.
Independent replication, more precise reliability estimates, and prospective validation of clinical relevance are needed.

This study investigated longitudinal changes in the joint temporal complexity of bilateral FP and left or right sgACC time series in patients with depression undergoing aTMS and untreated healthy controls.
We used bivariate multiscale sample entropy (bMSE) to quantify joint temporal complexity across scale factors a1-a10 and summarized the profiles as bMSE complexity indices (bMSE-CIs).
The same bilateral FP time series was used for both sgACC sides.
The primary test was the Group × Time × sgACC Hemisphere interaction for bMSE-CI, assessing whether the between-group difference in longitudinal change differed between sgACC hemispheres.
The hemispheric analysis was not prospectively prespecified; no directional hypothesis was asserted.
Scale-specific interaction tests and correlations with clinical outcomes were exploratory.
Functional connectivity (FC), regional multiscale sample entropy (MSE), and the bilateral sgACC mean-signal readout were examined as secondary measures.
These analyses characterize longitudinal FP-sgACC dynamics without establishing treatment-specific causality, directed coupling, or clinical biomarker validity.
All 39 participants in this observational study were enrolled at the University Hospital of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy Bern, encompassing both inpatient and outpatient populations.
Eligible patients were aged 18-65 years, presented with a current depressive episode, and were scheduled for TMS therapy.

The patient cohort (n = 24) included individuals with major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder with current depression (moderate to severe) according to DSM-5 criteria by the American Psychiatric Association (APA, 2013).
Patients with unipolar and bipolar depression were analyzed together because they shared a current depressive episode and the study focused on longitudinal FP-sgACC network dynamics during treatment.
Exclusion criteria comprised psychotic or neurological disorders, substance use disorders (excluding nicotine), claustrophobia, pregnancy, and contraindications to 7-Tesla MRI.
Healthy control participants (n = 15) were additionally required to have no current or lifetime psychiatric diagnosis.
All study participants provided written informed consent, and the study protocol was approved by the cantonal ethics committee of Bern, Switzerland (KEK: 2023-00134).

text.text: Treatment comprised 10 treatment days (Monday-Friday over 2 weeks), with four iTBS runs per day separated by reported 15-minute inter-run intervals, yielding 40 runs in total.

This study identified an exploratory group-dependent hemispheric difference in longitudinal FP-sgACC joint temporal complexity during aTMS.
Mean bMSE-CI decreased for the left sgACC pair and increased for the right pair in patients, whereas controls showed increases on both sides.
Because the same bilateral FP signal was used in both pairs, the hemispheric comparison concerns the sgACC component.
The findings describe longitudinal differences between patients and untreated controls; the observational design does not establish that aTMS caused these differences.
The direct three-way interaction supports a difference between groups in the hemispheric pattern of change, but its statistical significance depended on model specification.
The participantlevel contrast remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, and motion change, whereas random-intercept-only mixed models did not reach significance (p ≈ 0.072).
These approaches impose different within-participant covariance assumptions, so the results provide qualified evidence for the hemispheric effect.

The left-pair baseline group difference and the absence of FDR-significant within-group CI changes also caution against interpreting the interaction as a demonstrated treatment-induced reduction in patients.
Replication should assess the longitudinal contrast while accounting for baseline variability.
The a2 interaction survived FDR correction across all ten scales and identifies a difference at a fine temporal aggregation scale.

With TR = 1 s, a2 represents a 2-s aggregation window applied to BOLD signals already filtered to 0.008-0.09 Hz; it does not identify an isolated physiological frequency band or establish high-frequency neural activity, neural criticality, or excitation-inhibition balance.
The integrated CI and scale-specific analyses summarize different aspects of the entropy profile, and the a2 result does not imply that this scale alone accounts for the CI interaction.
The secondary FC and regional MSE analyses detected no Group × Time interactions, while one baseline association between right-pair FC and a1 bMSE survived FDR correction.
These results help characterize the measures but do not establish superior sensitivity of bMSE or independence from FC and regional MSE.
In particular, the secondary readout-specific tests address different hypotheses from the primary three-way interaction.
FC summarizes linear covariation, whereas bMSE evaluates the joint temporal complexity of embedded regional signals (McDonough & Nashiro, 2014; Wang et al., 2018).

Several limitations constrain interpretation.
The modest sample size limits precision and generalizability, and the hemispheric analysis was not prospectively prespecified.
Test-retest reliability in the 15 controls was uncertain: bMSE-CI ICC estimates were 0.422 for the left pair and -0.141 for the right pair, with broad confidence intervals.
These estimates limit confidence in individual change measurement and do not establish suitability for treatment monitoring.
No clinical bMSE association survived the specified FDR corrections.
The absence of a shamtreated patient group leaves habituation, time effects, and nonspecific treatment effects as alternative explanations.
Medication exposure and changes, diagnostic heterogeneity, and residual head motion may also contribute.

The unequal spatial extent of FP and sgACC masks may affect signal-to-noise ratio and entropy estimates, while entropy remains sensitive to spectral composition despite the refined-composite estimator.
Acquisition at 7 Tesla offers potential signal-to-noise advantages (Pohmann et al., 2016), but susceptibility-related distortion and signal dropout in the sgACC remain possible sources of bias.

text.text: In conclusion, bMSE identified an exploratory hemisphere-dependent longitudinal difference in FP-sgACC joint temporal complexity between patients undergoing aTMS and untreated healthy controls.
The integrated CI interaction and the FDR-corrected a2 interaction motivate further evaluation of bMSE as a candidate measure of longitudinal neural change in depression.
